newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: U.N. observers held hostage in Tajikistan freed.
newsitem.headline: U.N. observers held hostage in Tajikistan freed.

text.p: A rebel Tajik guerrilla group on Saturday freed seven United Nations military observers it had threatened to kill and 14 other hostages, diplomatic sources said.
The rebels continued to hold two members of the Tajik opposition, the sources said.
The United Nations said earlier that the captives included two Bulgarians, a Dane, a Jordanian, a Ukrainian, a Uruguayan and an Austrian.
The rebel group maintained demands for the release of four prisoners allied to their group before freeing the last two hostages, the sources said.
The rebels, who say they are loyal to field commander Rizvon Sadirov, released their hostages at about 5 p.m. local time (1200 GMT) after a government delegation held talks with the rebels.
They had threatened to shoot their hostages and detonate 30 bombs hidden around the capital Dushanbe unless their demands were met by two p.m. (0900 GMT) on Sunday.
They also said Russian border guards, thousands of whom have a peacekeeping role in Tajikistan, must provide safe passage for Sadirov's fighters to join them from bases across the Afghan border.
The U.N. mission has 96 foreign military observers in Tajikistan. Its mandate was renewed last week for four months.
U.N. observers have twice this month been subject to beatings or mock executions at the hands of Tajik government soldiers.
A U.N. source said the guerrillas held up a column carrying a joint delegation of U.N. personnel, Tajik officials and members of the armed Islamic opposition on Friday.
Amirkul Azimov, Secretary of Tajikistan's Security Council, told Reuters in Dushanbe earlier that the guerrillas had agreed to free all hostages after all-night talks.

Sadirov had until recently been allied with the Islamic rebel opposition to Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov, but switched to back the government of the former Soviet republic, apparently without surrendering control of his forces.
Tens of thousands of people have been killed in the civil war between Tajikistan's secular government and Islamist guerrillas.
In Moscow, separate talks aimed at ending Tajikistan's four-year civil war between Rakhmonov and opposition delegation head Sayid Abdullo Nuri continued without any apparent result.
Rakhmonov's press secretary, Zafar Saidov, told Itar-Tass news agency no peace accord would be signed on Saturday, as had been expected, and experts would try to prepare it by Monday.
"If the dialogue breaks down, the situation could become uncontrollable which would aggravate the military and political situation up to renewal of the war," he said.
The negotiations are being mediated by Russia and the United Nations.

Itar-Tass quoted Russian Foreign Ministry spokesman Mikhail Demurin as saying a peace agreement had not been signed "because of the refusal of the Tajik opposition to sign earlier agreed to documents."
